You say where you live, which languages you speak, what you like and what’s in town.
To conjugate -ER verbs (parler, habiter, aimer) in the present.
To say where you live: J’habite à… / en… / au…
To say which languages you speak and how well.
To say what you like and don’t like: aimer, adorer, détester + le / la / les.
To use the contractions au, aux, du, des.
Ioana’s first weekend in Lyon. She’s strolling through the market on the banks of the Saône and runs into Julien.
Ioana! Hi! Do you live nearby?
Hi, Julien! Yes, I live on Rue Mercière. And you?
I live near the station. But I love the market on Saturdays.
Me too! I like the fruit and the flowers.
Thanks, but I still speak a bit slowly. I also speak English and Italian.
Three languages! I only speak French… and a little English.
No, I don’t work on Saturdays. Do you like cheese?
Yes, a lot! But I hate cheese that’s too strong.
Then taste this saint-marcellin. It’s Lyon’s cheese.
Mmm… It’s delicious! Shall we eat at a café afterwards?
Good idea. There’s a nice café near the museum.
With -ER verbs, the endings -e, -es and -ent are NOT pronounced at all! “je parle, tu parles, ils parlent” all sound like “parl”. Only nous (-ons) and vous (-ez) have endings you can hear.
-ER (infinitive), -EZ and É are all a closed “e”, like “ay” in “day”: parler = “par-LAY”, vous parlez = “voo par-LAY”, musée = “mu-ZAY”.
H is never pronounced. With “habiter” you get elision and liaison: j’habite = “zha-BEET”, nous habitons = “noo-za-bee-TÕ”.
GN is read “ny”, as in “canyon”: montagne = “mõ-TANY”, Avignon = “a-vee-NYÕ”.
OI is read “wa”: moi = “mwa”, toi = “twa”, trois = “trwa”.
EAU and AU are read “o”: beaucoup = “bo-KOO”, au café = “o ka-FAY”.
Almost 90% of French verbs end in -ER and are all conjugated the same way. If you learn “parler”, you know hundreds of verbs: habiter, aimer, travailler, regarder, écouter…
The rule: drop -ER and add the ending for the person.
“Ils parlent” is read “eel parl”, NOT “parlent” with “ent”. The verb ending -ent is always silent. It’s beginners’ mistake number one.
The good news: when you speak, four of the six forms sound identical! To conjugate correctly out loud you only need three sounds: “parl”, “par-LÕ”, “par-LAY”.
With verbs starting with a vowel or h, “je” becomes “j’”: j’habite, j’aime, j’écoute, j’adore.
2. Where you live: à, en, au
For “in” a city or a country, French has three words, depending on the kind of place:
J’habite à Lyon. J’habite à Iași.
feminine country (most of them, ending in -e)
en France, en Roumanie, en Italie
au Canada, au Japon, au Portugal
Tip: almost all countries ending in -e are feminine → “en”. Famous exception: le Mexique → au Mexique.
For a street you don’t need a preposition: “J’habite rue Mercière” (I live on Rue Mercière).
Languages are masculine and written with a small letter. After “parler” the article is optional:
I’m learning French. (with other verbs: with the article)
I speak a little Romanian and a lot of English.
French “aimer” works like English “like”: the person who feels is the subject: “J’aime le café” = “I like coffee”.
After aimer, adorer, détester, préférer you ALWAYS use the definite article, even where English has none: “J’aime le café”, “J’adore les chats”. Never “J’aime café”.
Surprise: “J’aime bien” is WEAKER than “J’aime”. About a person, “Je t’aime” = “I love you”, whereas “Je t’aime bien” = “I like you / you’re nice”.
With verbs too: “J’aime voyager” (I like travelling). The second verb stays in the infinitive.
When “à” (to, at) or “de” (of, from) meets “le” or “les”, they merge into one word. With “la” and “l’” nothing changes.
We eat at the café. (à + le café)
There’s a café near the museum. (de + le musée)
I’m going to the bakery. (no change)
“À le” and “de le” don’t exist! Always say “au” and “du”.
It works just like with ÊTRE and AVOIR: ne + verb + pas.
“Le samedi” (with the article) = every Saturday. “Samedi” (no article) = this Saturday. The days of the week come in chapter 4.
France is a feminine country → en.
After aimer comes the definite article.
ne + aime + pas, with the article “le”.
There’s a café near the museum.
There’s a nice café near the museum.
Sophie, la boulangère qui parle vite
Sophie is forty. She has always lived in Lyon. She works in a little bakery on Rue Saint-Jean.
She starts work very early: at four in the morning! She makes the bread and the croissants.
Sophie loves talking. She talks to all the customers: tourists, students, the old ladies of the neighbourhood.
But she speaks very, very fast! The tourists don’t always understand.
Ioana has a problem too: in the morning she only understands “bonjour” and “merci”.
One day Ioana says: “Sophie, please speak slowly. I’m Romanian and I’m learning French.”
Sophie laughs: “Oh, sorry! I don’t speak Romanian. I only speak French… and a little Italian, for the pizzas!”
Now, with Ioana, Sophie speaks slowly. And Ioana understands everything.
